title: Public Relations as a Function of Corporate Communication: A Comparative Analysis of Role Differentiation and Professional Identity
content: Purpose – This study examines whether public relations (PR) operate as a subordinate subset of corporate communication (CC) or as an autonomous strategic function, and tests how the structural positioning of PR is associated with practitioner identity, legitimacy and influence across institutional contexts. Design/methodology/approach – A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design combines a survey of 612 PR/CC professionals in Anglo-American, European and Asia-Pacific multinationals—analyzed through structural equation modeling, measurement invariance testing and latent profile analysis—with Foucauldian discourse analysis of 412 job descriptions and 60 organizational charts. Findings – Structural autonomy is associated with strategic professional identity (β = 0.54) and coalition access with perceived legitimacy (β = 0.58); role ambiguity partially mediates the structure–authority link, and boundary-spanning intensity moderates’ structure–identity effects. Path strengths vary by region (β = 0.62, 0.47 and 0.39), and a four-profile typology—Strategic Autonomous, Integrated CC Subordinated, Hybrid Distributed and Marginalized Tactical—is consistent with the Recursive Legitimacy Model of PR Positioning (RLM-PRP). Research limitations/implications – The cross-sectional design supports associational rather than causal inference, the non-probability sample and three-region scope limit generalization, and the recursive loop awaits longitudinal testing. Practical implications – Durable gains in PR’s standing require organizational-design interventions—formalized coalition access, jurisdictional clarification and investment in boundary spanning—alongside individual-level development. Originality/value – The study integrates role, boundary-spanning, professionalization and power-dynamic theories into a testable model of how PR’s structural positioning shape’s professional identity, and offers a parsimonious, cross-regionally validated typology for diagnosing communication functions.
